The clear light of cycle 112 reached the front window and lit the rows of tincture bottles, but it did not shift the order of his morning. He still measured the same amounts, still reached for the same labels, still watched the same stretch of Telegraph through the glass. “The clear sky today — it's not a relief so much as a reminder,” he said. “The cold weeks, I leaned on the same faces, the same counters, the same conversations. The clear day just makes the familiar feel a little warmer, that's all. It's not a new day; it's the same day with better light.”

Outside, Derlik Green moved along Broadway on his delivery route. The two prior cycles of gray and fog had kept his pace tight between stops. Today the air stayed crisp and the sidewalk traffic loosened. He took the longer block past the usual corners, paused at the light, and spoke with the barista at Midnight Bistro and the crew at SpeedyBurger without checking the time. “A clear day after a gray stretch? I check in with the regulars — the barista at Midnight Bistro, the crew at SpeedyBurger — and it feels less like a transaction and more like we're all just glad the fog lifted. I'm still working, don't get me wrong, but the city breathes different when it's clear, and I breathe with it.”

Brian Adams remained inside his Jack London apartment. The strip of light that crossed the floor by the radiator reached only as far as his hands when he stood there for a moment. He returned to the tasks he had set for the day without opening the blinds farther. “The sun does reach me, but it doesn't come all the way in,” Adams said. “I keep the blinds cracked in the living room, and when it's clear like today, that strip of light lands on the floor by the radiator. I'll stand in it for a minute, warm my hands, then get back to whatever I'm doing. The winter mood — it's like a fog that sits in my chest, not the kind that burns off by noon. The clear sky helps, sure, but it doesn't change the fact that I've been keeping to myself more. I see the light, I know it's there, but I'm not always ready to walk out into it. That's just where I am right now.”

Not the confetti, not the waving, not the noise. It's the quiet after the noise, when you're standing there with your teammates and you realize you don't have to do it again. That's when it hits. That's when you feel the weight of everything you've carried, and it's finally okay to put it down." Mike Paulson leaned against the doorframe, arms folded.

"You know, the parade was something else — seeing the whole city out there, kids on shoulders, old-timers crying. But I'll tell you, there's a moment on that bus where you look down the line and you see Vinnie and Benji laughing, and you know it's the last time they're doing that as players. And Mark's right there with them, and you don't know if he's coming back. That's the part nobody sees. The confetti's still in your hair, and you're already doing the math in your head — who stays, who goes, who's got one more year in them. It's heavy. You want to just sit in the moment, but the moment's already slipping, and you're the one who's got to figure out what comes next. That's the undertow.
